analysis.one_liner: Stops hospitals from billing patients out-of-network rates for emergencies unless patients agree in advance.
analysis.headline: Despite 37 cosponsors, the bill was never given a hearing or vote in either committee that controlled it, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would force hospitals, as a condition of participating in Medicare, to tell patients before treatment whether the hospital or any of its providers are outside their insurance network, and to estimate what the patient would owe. For scheduled care, a hospital could charge out-of-network rates only if the patient signed a consent form at least 24 hours beforehand. For emergency and same-day care, the hospital could never charge the patient more than what an in-network visit would cost. Congress never voted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Insured patients who land in an emergency room or a hospital where one of the doctors treating them is out of network — a common situation patients cannot control or detect in advance. The bill caps their bill at in-network cost-sharing for emergencies and requires clear disclosure and signed consent before any out-of-network charge for scheduled care.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Insured patients facing surprise hospital bills

how_it_helps.text: Hospitals must give patients written notice of whether the hospital or any treating provider is out of network, and if so, an estimate of what the patient will owe above normal in-network cost-sharing.

For scheduled, non-emergency services, a hospital may charge out-of-network rates only if the patient signs a consent form at least 24 hours before treatment, acknowledging that the charge will not count toward in-network deductibles or out-of-pocket limits.

For emergency and same-day services, the hospital and its providers may not charge the patient more than the amount that would apply if the care were in-network — the patient cannot be stuck with the out-of-network difference.
The rules are enforced by making compliance a condition of participating in Medicare, so a hospital that keeps surprise-billing patients risks its Medicare agreement.

analysis.who_pays: Hospitals and the physicians who bill patients independently at hospitals — especially emergency-room, anesthesia, and other staffing physicians — would lose a large revenue stream: their ability to charge out-of-network patients the difference between billed charges and what insurance pays.

drawbacks.text: The bill does not flatly ban out-of-network charges for scheduled care: a patient who signs the consent form can still be billed the estimated out-of-network amount, which can be large, and the protection depends on a patient reading and understanding an estimate 24 hours in advance.

It covers only hospitals and critical access hospitals, including providers billing through them — freestanding facilities and ground ambulance services, a well-known gap in surprise-billing protections, are not addressed.

The bill limits what patients pay but does not set how much insurers must pay out-of-network providers, leaving the underlying dispute between hospitals, staffing physicians, and insurers unresolved, and cutting into hospital and physician revenue that supports some safety-net services.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protections are real but narrower than a full ban: strong for emergencies, weaker for scheduled care where a signed consent form can still leave a patient owing a large out-of-network bill, and silent on ambulances and freestanding facilities. The cost falls on hospitals and hospital-based physicians who profit from out-of-network billing, though some of that revenue pays for services that could come under pressure. On balance, a worthwhile but incomplete fix that a more comprehensive bill later addressed.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means and Energy and Commerce committees, then to a health subcommittee, and neither committee ever held a markup or vote on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on January 30, 2019 by Rep. Lloyd Doggett with 37 Democratic cosponsors and no Republican cosponsors.
It was referred to the Ways and Means Committee and the Energy and Commerce Committee, and then to the Health Subcommittee.
No further action — no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote — was ever recorded, and the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hospitals and out-of-network hospital-based physicians kept the ability to surprise-bill patients for the rest of the Congress. Congress ultimately passed its own broader surprise-billing ban in December 2020 as part of a year-end spending law, so patients did eventually get federal protections — but through different legislation, not this one.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Hospitals, which kept surprise-billing for two more years

for.name: Rep. Lloyd Doggett
for.what_they_did: Introduced the End Surprise Billing Act of 2019 on January 30, 2019.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled a markup or vote before the Congress ended.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled a markup or vote before the Congress ended.

against.name: Hospital and physician-staffing industries
against.what_they_did: Ran a well-publicized lobbying campaign against strong surprise-billing protections, favoring weaker alternatives, as Congress considered competing bills.

sides.party_line_note: All 38 sponsors and cosponsors were House Democrats — 37 of 231, with no Republican signing on — even though surprise-billing legislation overall drew bipartisan interest that Congress and the administration pursued through other vehicles.

industries.note: Hospitals lose the ability to charge out-of-network patients above in-network cost-sharing for emergencies, and to charge out-of-network rates for scheduled care without signed consent 24 hours ahead. That billed difference is currently paid by patients out of pocket.

industries.industry: Hospital-based physician staffing companies (emergency, anesthesia, radiology)
industries.note: These firms bill patients separately and often out of network even at in-network hospitals; the bill caps what their patients can be charged and makes disclosure and consent mandatory. Many are backed by private equity, which has a direct stake in out-of-network billing revenue.
Capping patient liability for out-of-network care reduces the surprise bills insurers' customers face and eases billing disputes, without requiring insurers to expand their networks.
